screens.title: Reading Blockchain Data: Blocks, Transactions, Events
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you'll learn how to read and monitor Ethereum data with Web3. js. Reading the chain means fetching block metadata, inspecting individual transactions, and listening for contract events. These skills let your application show live balances, transaction history, and react to contract activity as it happens. We'll cover fetching a block by number or hash, deciding when to request full transaction objects, and using a WebSocket provider to subscribe to new block headers, pending transactions, and contract logs. You will also see concrete code examples used with a local test node like Ganache and learn the common mistake of using an HTTP provider for subscriptions. By the end you will be able to implement both one-off queries for analytics and continuous subscriptions for live updates. This matters because correct reading patterns reduce bandwidth, avoid null results for unmined transactions, and make your dApp resilient to network differences between HTTP and WebSocket providers. Ready to explore block structure, transaction details, and event logs and build a small monitor script? Let’s begin and make sure your app reads the blockchain efficiently and reliably.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Outcomes
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide connects the techniques to real application features. When you can fetch the latest block number and blocks by hash, your dApp can display live blockchain progress and block-level analytics. When you can fetch transactions and interpret the block number field, your UI can indicate whether a transaction is pending, mined, or not found. Subscriptions let you implement features like live activity feeds, mempool indicators, or in-app notifications for contract events. Subscribing to contract logs with an ABI allows you to filter for events like token transfers or custom notifications and react immediately. A common misconception is that subscriptions are always identical across providers; in practice, not every node supports WebSockets or the same range of topics, so your code should fail gracefully. These outcomes matter because users expect real-time feedback and accurate status. Practicing with Ganache gives you a controlled environment to test these flows before you move to a public WebSocket endpoint.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Learning Objectives
Feature mapping
  • Block queries → block explorers, confirmations counters, and block timestamp displays.
  • Transaction reads → transaction details pages and confirmation status indicators.
  • Pending tx subscriptions → mempool visualizers and pending-tx alerts.

Mnemonic

screens.title: What is a Block and what it contains
screens.narratorSegment: A block is the fundamental unit of the Ethereum ledger: it bundles a set of transactions with a timestamp, a miner address, a reference to the previous block, and additional metadata. Knowing which fields to read matters for both analytics and live UIs. For example, the block's number and timestamp let you calculate confirmations and show when a block was mined. The transactions array can either contain only transaction hashes or full transaction objects depending on how you call the method. Requesting full transaction objects is useful when you immediately need sender, recipient, or value fields, but it costs more bandwidth and latency. A practical pattern is to fetch the block with only hashes to get lightweight counts for dashboards, then request individual transactions as needed. A common misconception is to always request full transactions; this can slow down the UI and increase RPC costs. Example: call getBlockNumber to find the latest index, then use getBlock with the number and false to quickly count transactions. Key takeaway: choose between transaction hashes or full objects based on the data your UI needs and the performance trade-offs. How will you decide when to fetch full transactions in your app?

keyIdea.title: Block structure
keyIdea.text: Blocks contain metadata and transactions. Request full transaction objects only when you need per-transaction details to save bandwidth.

content.html:
Definition
Block
A block is a batch of transactions plus a timestamp and a link to the previous block. It is the basis for confirmations and block-level analytics.
When to request full transactions
  • Request full objects when you need fields like from, to, value, or input data immediately.
  • Use hashes-only to get transaction counts or when you will lazily fetch details per item.
  • Balance the cost: full objects increase RPC payload size and parsing time.
Example
Use getBlockNumber to retrieve the latest index, then call getBlock(latestNumber, false) to get lightweight info and count transactions. Fetch full transactions on demand.
Visual: Block fields
Metadata
hash, parentHash, number, timestamp, miner
Transactions
Array of hashes or full transaction objects depending on the call.
Key Takeaway
Fetch hashes-only for counts and fetch full transactions selectively to avoid heavy RPC responses.

screens.title: Fetching the latest block and inspecting fields
screens.narratorSegment: Start by fetching the latest block number; this is the simplest query and gives you a stable anchor for further reads. After you have the number, call the getBlock method with that identifier. If you only need the transaction count, pass a second parameter of false to receive only transaction hashes; request true for full transaction objects if you need from, to, or value immediately. In a local test node like Ganache, this pattern helps you avoid heavy responses for UI components such as block lists. A concrete example: get the latest number, then call getBlock with that number and log the hash, timestamp (converted to a human time), miner, and transactions length. A common misconception is assuming getBlock will always return full transaction objects; by default you control that with the second parameter. When you fetch the timestamp, convert Unix seconds to a readable date for display. Practice: run a simple script that prints the latest block details and verifies the transaction array length. That exercise will clarify when to request full objects and how to show concise block metadata in your UI.

keyIdea.title: Practical fetch
keyIdea.text: Use getBlockNumber then getBlock with the appropriate fullTransactions option to balance detail and performance.

content.html:
Code: Read latest block
<!-- Node script example --> const Web3 = require('web3'); const web3 = new Web3('http://127.0.0.1:7545'); async function readLatest() { const latest = await web3.eth.getBlockNumber(); const block = await web3.eth.getBlock(latest, false); // false = hashes only console.log('Block:', block.number); console.log('Hash:', block.hash); console.log('Timestamp:', new Date(block.timestamp * 1000).toLocaleString()); console.log('Miner:', block.miner); console.log('Tx count:', block.transactions.length); } readLatest();
Explanation
  • getBlockNumber returns the latest block index quickly for navigation or polling.
  • getBlock with fullTransactions=false is efficient for counts and metadata-only displays.
  • Convert the Unix timestamp to a local date string before presenting to users.
Concrete scenario
Your explorer shows the last 20 blocks. Fetch only hashes to populate the list quickly, then load transaction details when the user opens a block detail view.
Key Takeaway

Choose lightweight reads for lists and fetch full transaction objects only when the UI requires them.

screens.title: Transaction details and inclusion status
screens.narratorSegment: A transaction is a signed instruction that changes state on Ethereum, such as transferring Ether or invoking a smart contract. When you call the getTransaction method with a transaction hash, you receive fields like from, to, value, gas price, and block number. The block number is the crucial field for inclusion: if it is null, the transaction is still pending or not yet mined. This is a common source of confusion — developers sometimes expect immediate details for newly broadcast transactions, but nodes may not have indexed them yet or they may be dropped from the mempool. One practical approach is to subscribe to pending transactions and then poll getTransaction until the block number is populated. Another approach is optimistic UI patterns that mark a transaction pending and update the UI when a block includes it. Example: when getTransaction returns null, show a pending state and retry after a short delay. Misconception: a null return means the transaction is invalid; instead it usually means it has not been mined or is not known to that node. Close by asking: how will your app differentiate between pending and failed transactions?

keyIdea.title: Transaction clarity
keyIdea.text: getTransaction returns transaction fields; a null block number indicates the transaction is not yet mined and should be handled as pending.

content.html:
Definition
Transaction
A signed message that changes state. Use getTransaction to read its fields and determine mining status.
Fields to inspect
  • from, to — who sent and who receives
  • value — amount transferred (in Wei)
  • gasPrice — execution cost per unit
  • blockNumber — null means pending or not found
Example workflow
Subscribe to pending transactions, show a pending badge in the UI when you detect the hash, then poll getTransaction until blockNumber is set and you can mark it confirmed. If getTransaction returns null repeatedly, treat it as not found and inform the user.
Common mistake
Interpreting null as failure. Null usually means unmined or unknown; verify by polling or waiting for a new block header to include the transaction.

screens.title: Subscribe to new block headers
screens.narratorSegment: Subscriptions let your dApp receive chain updates the moment they occur. To receive new block headers, you must connect to a WebSocket provider because HTTP providers do not support persistent subscriptions. The sequence is straightforward: initialize a Web3 instance with a WebSocket provider, call the subscribe method with the event name newBlockHeaders, and attach handlers for connected, data, and error events. On each received header, you typically log the block number and hash, then optionally fetch the full block details if you need transaction counts or metadata. Remember to clear subscriptions on shutdown to avoid resource leaks. A common misconception is that WebSocket subscriptions always deliver full blocks; they deliver headers — if you need transaction counts you may fetch the block after receiving the header. Example: when a header arrives, convert the timestamp and call getBlock(header. number, false) for a quick transaction count. This pattern powers live block explorers and confirmation trackers. How will your app handle temporary disconnections or reconnect attempts? Subscribe to new block headers means use a websocket provider and subscribe to newblockheaders, then fetch additional block details on demand to power live features.. In practical terms, set up a websocket subscription to receive new block headers in real time. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Subscription pattern
keyIdea.text: Use a WebSocket provider and subscribe to newBlockHeaders, then fetch additional block details on demand to power live features.

content.html:
Steps to subscribe
  1. Initialize Web3 with a WebSocket provider URL.
  2. Call web3.eth.subscribe with 'newBlockHeaders'.
  3. Attach handlers: on connected, on data, on error.
  4. Optionally fetch full block data after receiving the header.
Concrete example
Connect to ws://127.0.0.1:7545 in Ganache, subscribe to newBlockHeaders, and log block numbers as they arrive. This immediately powers live block counters and explorer updates.
Visual: subscription events
Connected → Data → Error
Handle network events, fetch block details when needed, and clear subscriptions on exit.
Pro tip

Keep subscriptions light: use headers as triggers and fetch heavy details only when required to keep your app responsive.

screens.title: Pending transactions subscription
screens.narratorSegment: Monitoring pending transactions gives you visibility into the mempool and enables features like pending transaction indicators or mempool visualizers. Use a WebSocket provider and subscribe to pendingTransactions. The subscription returns transaction hashes as they appear in the mempool; these hashes may not immediately resolve to full transaction objects via getTransaction because nodes may not have indexed the data yet. A robust approach is to treat the incoming hash as a signal: record it, show a pending badge, and then attempt to fetch details. If getTransaction returns null, retry after a short backoff. Some pending transactions will never be mined, so implement a timeout or a maximum number of retries. Example: on receiving a pending hash, log it and call getTransaction; if the transaction appears with a block number, mark it confirmed. A common misconception is that pending subscription delivers full transaction details; it only delivers hashes. This behavior conserves bandwidth but requires an extra fetch for details. When building a UI, consider how you display temporary or stale mempool data to avoid confusing users. Pending transactions subscription means pendingtransactions subscriptions deliver hashes. use them as signals and fetch full details only when available, with retries and timeouts for robustness.. In practical terms, monitor the mempool and react to pending transaction hashes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Mempool handling
keyIdea.text: pendingTransactions subscriptions deliver hashes. Use them as signals and fetch full details only when available, with retries and timeouts for robustness.

content.html:
Subscription behavior
Pending transaction subscriptions stream transaction hashes as they enter the node's mempool. Use these as triggers to fetch details and update UI state to pending.
Recommended flow
  1. Subscribe to pendingTransactions via WebSocket.
  2. On hash arrival, display a pending indicator immediately.
  3. Attempt to fetch details via getTransaction with retries and timeouts.
Concrete example
When you see a pending hash, show it in an activity feed with a spinner and later replace the spinner with confirmed details when getTransaction returns a block number.
Warning

Don't assume all pending hashes will be mined. Provide timeouts and clear UI guidance for pending entries.

screens.title: Subscribing to smart contract events
screens.narratorSegment: Smart contract events are structured logs that contracts emit to make important state changes discoverable. To subscribe to contract events you need the contract's ABI and its deployed address. Initialize a Web3 instance with a WebSocket provider and instantiate a contract object with the ABI and address. Then call the events A P I or subscribe to logs for the contract name or topics. Indexed parameters in Solidity events enable efficient filtering: if an event indexes a user address, you can request only events that include that address to reduce noise. A practical example: a ValueChanged event that indexes the user address allows your UI to subscribe only to changes for a specific user, keeping the client-side processing light. A common mistake is using an incorrect ABI or wrong contract address, which yields no events. Also remember to set fromBlock to latest when you only want new events. This pattern enables reactive dApp features like live balance updates or user notifications tied to contract state changes. Subscribing to smart contract events means use the contract abi and address with a websocket-enabled web3 instance to subscribe to events and filter via indexed parameters.. In practical terms, use abi and address to listen for contract logs and filter indexed parameters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Event subscriptions
keyIdea.text: Use the contract ABI and address with a WebSocket-enabled Web3 instance to subscribe to events and filter via indexed parameters.

content.html:
Setup
Create a Web3 instance with WebsocketProvider, then create a contract object with the ABI and address. Use contract.events.EventName or contract.getPastEvents and contract.events to subscribe to live events.
Filtering with indexed params
Solidity allows marking event parameters as indexed to enable efficient filtering. Set the event filter options to listen only for matching indexed values, which reduces client-side processing and network traffic.
Example event
ValueChanged(address indexed user, uint oldValue, uint newValue)
Subscribe with filter { user: '0x...' } to receive only events for that user.
Key Takeaway
Correct ABI, address, and topic filters are required for reliable event subscriptions. Use indexed parameters to stay efficient.

screens.title: HTTP vs WebSocket providers
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing the right provider matters. HTTP providers are simple and work well for one-off RPC calls such as getBlock, getTransaction, or getBalance. They are easy to scale, compatible with REST-like tooling, and reliable for occasional polling. WebSocket providers are required for real-time subscriptions such as newBlockHeaders or pendingTransactions because they support persistent bi-directional connections. A frequent mistake is attempting to call subscribe with an HTTP provider; subscriptions will fail with a network error because HTTP cannot maintain the persistent channel subscriptions need. Use HTTP for background analytics or occasional queries, and WebSocket when you need push updates. Another practical consideration: public WebSocket endpoints may have rate limits or connection policies; plan for reconnection logic and graceful degradation. Example: use HTTP to fetch the latest block number on a periodic poll and use WebSocket to receive new headers for immediate UI updates. The key is combining both providers when your architecture demands both historical reads and live updates. HTTP vs WebSocket providers means http is fine for snapshots and polls; websocket is required for persistent subscriptions. don’t try subscribing over http.. screens.title: Event logs and indexed parameters
screens.narratorSegment: Event logs are a contract-level mechanism to record structured data on the chain in a searchable form. Solidity allows marking event parameters as indexed so the logs are stored with topics that can be filtered efficiently by nodes. When you subscribe to contract events, you can pass filters that match indexed parameter values — for example, an indexed user address — and receive only events relevant to that filter. This lowers client-side processing and network noise. An important detail is that non-indexed parameters are stored in the event data blob and are not efficient for filtering; you should index the fields you plan to filter on. A common mistake is expecting arbitrary fields to be filterable; only indexed parameters and topics are supported for efficient server-side filtering. Example: a transfer event often indexes the sender and recipient so wallets can subscribe to transfers involving a particular address. When designing your contract A P I and front-end subscriptions, choose which parameters to index based on expected filters to keep event subscriptions practical and performant. Event logs and indexed parameters means index the fields you plan to filter for at contract design time, and subscribe using those indexed values to receive only relevant logs.. screens.title: Common mistakes and debugging tips
screens.narratorSegment: When building readers and subscribers, developers encounter a few recurring mistakes. First, attempting to subscribe with an HTTP provider results in network or unsupported-operation errors — always use a WebSocket provider for subscriptions. Second, requesting full transaction objects for every block can significantly increase latency and payload sizes; prefer hashes-first for lists. Third, treat getTransaction returning null as a sign of pending or unknown transaction rather than immediate failure. Implement retries and sensible UI timeouts. Fourth, ensure ABI and contract address match exactly when subscribing to events; a mismatched ABI or address yields no logs. For debugging, reproduce the issue on a controlled node like Ganache where you can generate transactions and events, then instrument your script with connected and error handlers to get clear failure reasons. Include graceful teardown logic that clears subscriptions on process exit so orphaned sockets don't linger. Finally, design reconnection and exponential backoff strategies for production WebSocket endpoints. These practical checks will save time during development and reduce runtime surprises. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you'll learn how to read and monitor Ethereum data with Web3. js. Reading the chain means fetching block metadata, inspecting individual transactions, and listening for contract events. These skills let your application show live balances, transaction history, and react to contract activity as it happens. We'll cover fetching a block by number or hash, deciding when to request full transaction objects, and using a WebSocket provider to subscribe to new block headers, pending transactions, and contract logs. You will also see concrete code examples used with a local test node like Ganache and learn the common mistake of using an HTTP provider for subscriptions. By the end you will be able to implement both one-off queries for analytics and continuous subscriptions for live updates. This matters because correct reading patterns reduce bandwidth, avoid null results for unmined transactions, and make your dApp resilient to network differences between HTTP and WebSocket providers. Ready to explore block structure, transaction details, and event logs and build a small monitor script? Let’s begin and make sure your app reads the blockchain efficiently and reliably.

By the end of this chapter you'll be able to retrieve block details, inspect transactions, and set up real-time subscriptions using Web3. js. First, you'll learn how to call the method that returns the latest block number, and then fetch a block by number or hash, optionally requesting full transaction objects when you need them. Second, you'll learn how to fetch an individual transaction by its hash and interpret fields such as sender, recipient, value, gas price, and block inclusion. Third, you'll implement subscriptions over a WebSocket provider to listen for new block headers and pending transactions so your application reacts to chain changes as they occur. Finally, you'll learn how to subscribe to smart contract events using a contract ABI and filter logs by indexed parameters. Each objective includes a short explanation and a small mnemonic to help you remember the sequence from querying to subscribing. These skills matter because they let you build dashboards, explorers, and reactive dApps that are correct and efficient. You will practice with Ganache in the hands-on activity to make these ideas concrete.

This second objectives slide connects the techniques to real application features. When you can fetch the latest block number and blocks by hash, your dApp can display live blockchain progress and block-level analytics. When you can fetch transactions and interpret the block number field, your UI can indicate whether a transaction is pending, mined, or not found. Subscriptions let you implement features like live activity feeds, mempool indicators, or in-app notifications for contract events. Subscribing to contract logs with an ABI allows you to filter for events like token transfers or custom notifications and react immediately. A common misconception is that subscriptions are always identical across providers; in practice, not every node supports WebSockets or the same range of topics, so your code should fail gracefully. These outcomes matter because users expect real-time feedback and accurate status. Practicing with Ganache gives you a controlled environment to test these flows before you move to a public WebSocket endpoint.

A block is the fundamental unit of the Ethereum ledger: it bundles a set of transactions with a timestamp, a miner address, a reference to the previous block, and additional metadata. Knowing which fields to read matters for both analytics and live UIs. For example, the block's number and timestamp let you calculate confirmations and show when a block was mined. The transactions array can either contain only transaction hashes or full transaction objects depending on how you call the method. Requesting full transaction objects is useful when you immediately need sender, recipient, or value fields, but it costs more bandwidth and latency. A practical pattern is to fetch the block with only hashes to get lightweight counts for dashboards, then request individual transactions as needed. A common misconception is to always request full transactions; this can slow down the UI and increase RPC costs. Example: call getBlockNumber to find the latest index, then use getBlock with the number and false to quickly count transactions. Key takeaway: choose between transaction hashes or full objects based on the data your UI needs and the performance trade-offs. How will you decide when to fetch full transactions in your app?

Start by fetching the latest block number; this is the simplest query and gives you a stable anchor for further reads. After you have the number, call the getBlock method with that identifier. If you only need the transaction count, pass a second parameter of false to receive only transaction hashes; request true for full transaction objects if you need from, to, or value immediately. In a local test node like Ganache, this pattern helps you avoid heavy responses for UI components such as block lists. A concrete example: get the latest number, then call getBlock with that number and log the hash, timestamp (converted to a human time), miner, and transactions length. A common misconception is assuming getBlock will always return full transaction objects; by default you control that with the second parameter. When you fetch the timestamp, convert Unix seconds to a readable date for display. Practice: run a simple script that prints the latest block details and verifies the transaction array length. That exercise will clarify when to request full objects and how to show concise block metadata in your UI.

A transaction is a signed instruction that changes state on Ethereum, such as transferring Ether or invoking a smart contract. When you call the getTransaction method with a transaction hash, you receive fields like from, to, value, gas price, and block number. The block number is the crucial field for inclusion: if it is null, the transaction is still pending or not yet mined. This is a common source of confusion — developers sometimes expect immediate details for newly broadcast transactions, but nodes may not have indexed them yet or they may be dropped from the mempool. One practical approach is to subscribe to pending transactions and then poll getTransaction until the block number is populated. Another approach is optimistic UI patterns that mark a transaction pending and update the UI when a block includes it. Example: when getTransaction returns null, show a pending state and retry after a short delay. Misconception: a null return means the transaction is invalid; instead it usually means it has not been mined or is not known to that node. Close by asking: how will your app differentiate between pending and failed transactions?

Subscriptions let your dApp receive chain updates the moment they occur. To receive new block headers, you must connect to a WebSocket provider because HTTP providers do not support persistent subscriptions. The sequence is straightforward: initialize a Web3 instance with a WebSocket provider, call the subscribe method with the event name newBlockHeaders, and attach handlers for connected, data, and error events. On each received header, you typically log the block number and hash, then optionally fetch the full block details if you need transaction counts or metadata. Remember to clear subscriptions on shutdown to avoid resource leaks. A common misconception is that WebSocket subscriptions always deliver full blocks; they deliver headers — if you need transaction counts you may fetch the block after receiving the header. Example: when a header arrives, convert the timestamp and call getBlock(header. number, false) for a quick transaction count. This pattern powers live block explorers and confirmation trackers. How will your app handle temporary disconnections or reconnect attempts? Subscribe to new block headers means use a websocket provider and subscribe to newblockheaders, then fetch additional block details on demand to power live features.. In practical terms, set up a websocket subscription to receive new block headers in real time. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Monitoring pending transactions gives you visibility into the mempool and enables features like pending transaction indicators or mempool visualizers. Use a WebSocket provider and subscribe to pendingTransactions. The subscription returns transaction hashes as they appear in the mempool; these hashes may not immediately resolve to full transaction objects via getTransaction because nodes may not have indexed the data yet. A robust approach is to treat the incoming hash as a signal: record it, show a pending badge, and then attempt to fetch details. If getTransaction returns null, retry after a short backoff. Some pending transactions will never be mined, so implement a timeout or a maximum number of retries. Example: on receiving a pending hash, log it and call getTransaction; if the transaction appears with a block number, mark it confirmed. A common misconception is that pending subscription delivers full transaction details; it only delivers hashes. This behavior conserves bandwidth but requires an extra fetch for details. When building a UI, consider how you display temporary or stale mempool data to avoid confusing users. Pending transactions subscription means pendingtransactions subscriptions deliver hashes. use them as signals and fetch full details only when available, with retries and timeouts for robustness.. In practical terms, monitor the mempool and react to pending transaction hashes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Smart contract events are structured logs that contracts emit to make important state changes discoverable. To subscribe to contract events you need the contract's ABI and its deployed address. Initialize a Web3 instance with a WebSocket provider and instantiate a contract object with the ABI and address. Then call the events A P I or subscribe to logs for the contract name or topics. Indexed parameters in Solidity events enable efficient filtering: if an event indexes a user address, you can request only events that include that address to reduce noise. A practical example: a ValueChanged event that indexes the user address allows your UI to subscribe only to changes for a specific user, keeping the client-side processing light. A common mistake is using an incorrect ABI or wrong contract address, which yields no events. Also remember to set fromBlock to latest when you only want new events. This pattern enables reactive dApp features like live balance updates or user notifications tied to contract state changes. Subscribing to smart contract events means use the contract abi and address with a websocket-enabled web3 instance to subscribe to events and filter via indexed parameters.. In practical terms, use abi and address to listen for contract logs and filter indexed parameters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through a small terminal-style script that subscribes to new block headers and logs details. Choosing the right provider matters. HTTP providers are simple and work well for one-off RPC calls such as getBlock, getTransaction, or getBalance. They are easy to scale, compatible with REST-like tooling, and reliable for occasional polling. WebSocket providers are required for real-time subscriptions such as newBlockHeaders or pendingTransactions because they support persistent bi-directional connections. A frequent mistake is attempting to call subscribe with an HTTP provider; subscriptions will fail with a network error because HTTP cannot maintain the persistent channel subscriptions need. Use HTTP for background analytics or occasional queries, and WebSocket when you need push updates. Another practical consideration: public WebSocket endpoints may have rate limits or connection policies; plan for reconnection logic and graceful degradation. Example: use HTTP to fetch the latest block number on a periodic poll and use WebSocket to receive new headers for immediate UI updates. The key is combining both providers when your architecture demands both historical reads and live updates. Event logs are a contract-level mechanism to record structured data on the chain in a searchable form. Solidity allows marking event parameters as indexed so the logs are stored with topics that can be filtered efficiently by nodes. When you subscribe to contract events, you can pass filters that match indexed parameter values — for example, an indexed user address — and receive only events relevant to that filter. This lowers client-side processing and network noise. An important detail is that non-indexed parameters are stored in the event data blob and are not efficient for filtering; you should index the fields you plan to filter on. A common mistake is expecting arbitrary fields to be filterable; only indexed parameters and topics are supported for efficient server-side filtering. Example: a transfer event often indexes the sender and recipient so wallets can subscribe to transfers involving a particular address. When building readers and subscribers, developers encounter a few recurring mistakes. First, attempting to subscribe with an HTTP provider results in network or unsupported-operation errors — always use a WebSocket provider for subscriptions. Second, requesting full transaction objects for every block can significantly increase latency and payload sizes; prefer hashes-first for lists. Third, treat getTransaction returning null as a sign of pending or unknown transaction rather than immediate failure. Implement retries and sensible UI timeouts. Fourth, ensure ABI and contract address match exactly when subscribing to events; a mismatched ABI or address yields no logs. For debugging, reproduce the issue on a controlled node like Ganache where you can generate transactions and events, then instrument your script with connected and error handlers to get clear failure reasons. Remember three core ideas. First, blocks are collections of transactions plus metadata; choose whether to request full transaction objects based on your UI needs to avoid large payloads. Second, transactions returned by getTransaction include a block number that indicates inclusion; a null block number means the transaction is pending or not known to the node. Third, subscriptions require a WebSocket provider; use newBlockHeaders and pendingTransactions to power live updates, and use contract ABIs with indexed event parameters to filter logs efficiently.
